lesson.title: For Loops and Accumulators
lesson.objective: Read, predict and write for loops that build up a result with an accumulator variable.
lesson.approachReason: An accumulator is a small procedure with a fixed shape, best learned by watching a full trace, then a faded trace, then solving one alone.

blocks.heading: A loop that leaves something behind
blocks.body:
A for loop repeats lines of code, but on its own it leaves no trace when it finishes. Most useful loops do a job that outlasts them: adding up a bill, counting how many scores pass, gluing letters into a message.

To do that, the loop needs a variable created outside it and updated on every pass. That variable is called an accumulator.
blocks.example: A scoreboard behaves the same way: it shows 0 before the game, climbs as points are scored, and you read the final number after the final whistle.

blocks.heading: Trace the running total
blocks.prompt: Step through this loop and watch the variable total change on every pass.
blocks.code:
total = 0
for n in [3, 7, 2]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
blocks.explanation: total is created once, before the loop. The line total = total + n does not overwrite a new variable each time — it reads the old total, adds n, and stores the result back in the same box.
hints: Notice that line 3 runs three times but total is only created once.
After each pass, total holds the sum of everything seen so far.

trace.note: total is created and set to 0.
The loop starts and n is set to the first item of the list.
total becomes the old total plus n.
The loop goes back and takes the next item.
Last item of the list is picked up.
total becomes 10 + 2, then the list is finished.
The loop is over, so print runs once with the finished total.

blocks.heading: The accumulator pattern
blocks.body:
Every accumulator follows the same three moves, in this order: create it before the loop, update it inside the loop (usually acc = acc + something), and read it after the loop, when it holds the finished result.

The starting value matters. Use 0 for a sum or a count, 1 for a product, and an empty string "" for text you are building up. Start a sum at 1 and every answer will be wrong.
blocks.example: Summing [3, 7, 2]: total = 0 before the loop, total = total + n inside, print(total) after — 12.

hints: A NameError means Python was asked to use a name that does not exist yet.
Where does the name total first need to exist?
blocks.retry: Think of the accumulator as a jar. You must put an empty jar on the table before the loop starts tossing things in — otherwise the loop has nothing to add to.

blocks.heading: Worked example: counting, not summing

steps.title: Set up the counter
steps.why: A counter must exist before the loop and start empty, or the first count = count + 1 fails with a NameError.

steps.title: Pass 1: n = 4
steps.text: 4 > 5 is False, so the line inside the if does not run.

steps.title: Pass 3: n = 2
steps.text: 2 > 5 is False again, so nothing happens.

steps.title: Passes 4 and 5: n = 11, then 7
steps.text: Both pass the test, so count climbs 1 → 2 → 3.
steps.why: count = 3, and the list is exhausted, so the loop ends.

blocks.answer: print(count) shows 3 — the number of values above 5, not their sum (which would be 22).

hints: Follow one pass at a time. What does total hold at the end of the very first pass?
If total is wiped at the start of every pass, only the final item can survive.
blocks.retry: The loop body runs again and again. Anything at the top of the body is undone on every single pass, so a running total can never run.

hints: Ask what total holds the moment the first loop ends.
The second loop starts from that value, not from zero.
blocks.retry: An accumulator does not reset itself. It only restarts if you write total = 0 again — and sometimes keeping the old value is exactly what you want.

blocks.heading: Build a product on your own
blocks.prompt:
A loop runs over the list [2, 3, 5]. Before the loop: product = 1. Inside the loop: product = product * n. After the loop: print(product).

What does the program print? Type just the number.

traps.feedback: That is the sum 2 + 3 + 5. The line multiplies, so the numbers compound instead of adding.
That happens if you start the accumulator at 0 — the first multiply gives 0 and nothing can recover from it.
That is product after two passes only — the last number, 5, has not been multiplied in yet.

hints: Trace it pass by pass rather than spotting a pattern.
blocks.solution: product = 1 → 1 * 2 = 2 → 2 * 3 = 6 → 6 * 5 = 30, so print(product) shows 30. The start value of 1 is what makes a product accumulator work: starting at 0 would make every multiplication zero.

activities.title: Works or broken?
activities.prompt: Drag each snippet into the right bucket. "Works" means the loop ends with the correct finished result sitting in the accumulator.
activities.reveal: An accumulator needs three things in the right order: create it before the loop, update it inside the loop, and read it after the loop.

items.text: total = 0 before the loop; total = total + n inside the loop
total = total + n inside the loop, but total is never set before the loop
total = 0 as the first line inside the loop body, above the add line
count = 0 before the loop; inside an if, count = count + 1
count = count + 1 inside the loop; count = 0 after the loop
total = 0 before the loop; total = total + n inside; print(total) after the loop

activities.title: Predict the total
activities.prompt:
Before you run anything, work out what this prints:

total = 0
for n in [1, 2, 3, 4]:
    total = total + n * 2
print(total)

Which value does print show?
activities.reveal: Each pass adds n * 2 to the running total: 2, then 6, then 12, then 20. The accumulator keeps everything the earlier passes added.

options.feedback: Correct. The passes add 2, 4, 6 and 8 to a total that keeps growing: 2, 6, 12, 20.
That is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 — the accumulator is adding n * 2, not n.
That is the total after three passes. The last value, n = 4, still adds 8 more.
That double-counts. The total is not multiplied by 2; only each item is.

questions.question: Leo wants to add up every number in a list. Inside his loop he writes total = total + n, and the program crashes with a NameError on exactly that line. What should he do?
options: Create total = 0 on a line before the loop starts.
Move total = total + n to a line before the loop starts.
Change the for loop into a while loop.
Rename total to n so the two names match.
questions.correctAnswer: Create total = 0 on a line before the loop starts.
questions.explanation: An accumulator has to exist before the loop first uses it, and it needs a starting value — 0 for a sum. Without that setup line, Python has never seen the name total.

questions.question: Sam writes total = 0 on the line before his loop over [5, 10, 15], and total = total + n inside the loop. A classmate moves total = 0 to the first line inside the loop body, above the add line. What does print(total) show now?
questions.explanation: Resetting a variable inside the loop body wipes it on every pass, so the running total never survives. Only the last value added — 15 — is left at the end.

questions.question: Priya's loop over [2, 4, 6] starts with total = 0 and adds each number, ending at 12. Without resetting total, she then runs a second loop over [1, 1] using the same add line. What does print(total) show now?
questions.explanation: The accumulator keeps whatever value it held when the first loop ended. The second loop adds 1 and 1 on top of 12, giving 14.
